tldr: To solve the exploration bottleneck caused by massive muscle redundancy in musculoskeletal reinforcement learning, the authors propose intermittently holding and controlling the reflex threshold length $\lambda$ based on the equilibrium-point (EP) hypothesis. With only a minimal forward-velocity reward, the model learns human-like sprinting in just about one hour.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed $\lambda$-hold controller. The policy outputs per-muscle threshold lengths $\lambda$ only intermittently, synchronized with gait-phase events, and holds these values between decision points. Meanwhile, a stretch-reflex recruitment law automatically and coordinately computes muscle excitations $e$ mediated by skeletal dynamic coupling.
overview:
The human lower limb is actuated by far more muscles than its mechanical degrees of freedom, so countless muscle activation patterns can produce the exact same joint torque (the muscle redundancy problem). When training a reinforcement learning (RL) agent in this setting, exploring all muscle excitations independently at every time step causes action noise to cancel out in joint space. This leads to an "inefficient exploration problem" where learning completely stalls. Prior predictive simulations had to rely on motion-capture tracking rewards, complex metabolic cost functions, or hand-crafted reflex circuits.

To overcome this, the authors turned to two neurophysiological principles: the equilibrium-point (EP) hypothesis and intermittent control. Instead of directly exciting muscles, the policy issues a threshold length $\lambda$—the length above which a muscle starts to recruit and contract—only once every several steps, holding that value between decision points. Fine step-by-step muscle activations are handled autonomously by a local stretch-reflex law. Because muscles are mechanically interconnected through the skeleton, simply adjusting $\lambda$ independently naturally gives rise to coordinated, synergistic muscle action.

Using a 3D musculoskeletal model with 21 degrees of freedom and 90 muscles trained purely to maximize forward velocity, human-like sprinting at roughly $4.7\,$ m/s emerged in only about one hour of training. The resulting joint angle trajectories, ground reaction force profiles, and muscle activation timings match real human electromyography (EMG) closely, demonstrating both physiological validity and overwhelming sample efficiency.
contributions: Demonstrated for the first time that human-like sprinting can emerge from a minimal forward-velocity reward without motion imitation or symmetry rewards.

Dramatically improved exploration efficiency in muscle-redundant action spaces using $\lambda$-hold control, which takes the EP threshold length $\lambda$ as the control variable and updates it via gait-event-driven intermittent holds.
Enabled high-quality sprint learning in an exceptionally short training time of roughly one hour on a single workstation.
Offered a neurophysiologically interpretable framework rather than an ad-hoc engineering trick, unifying the EP hypothesis, intermittent control, and optimal feedback control.

sections.heading: Why is reinforcement learning so hard on musculoskeletal models?
sections.summary: Because of massive muscle redundancy, standard action noise in reinforcement learning cancels out in joint space, causing exploration to break down. Prior work relied on hand-crafted reflexes or complex reward shaping; this study resolves the root issue using the physiological equilibrium-point hypothesis.
sections.details:
Movement simulation of the human body broadly splits into inverse simulation, which computes muscle forces back from recorded kinematics, and predictive simulation, which generates forward motion emergently from a body model and a controller. Predictive simulation is far better for generalization and mechanistic understanding, but muscle-level control faces a formidable barrier.

That barrier is the muscle redundancy problem. Because muscles vastly outnumber mechanical degrees of freedom in the lower limbs, infinitely many muscle activation combinations yield identical joint moments. Conventional optimization approaches picked a single solution by minimizing squared activations or metabolic energy, but mathematically convenient optima do not necessarily match actual biological muscle activity (EMG).

In reinforcement learning, this manifests as an inefficient exploration problem. A standard RL agent explores by injecting independent Gaussian noise into every muscle's excitation at every step. Because the muscle-to-joint mapping is many-to-one, uncorrelated noise across antagonistic and synergistic muscles cancels out, failing to produce varied movements in joint space. The model simply collapses on the spot.

Previous work tackled this by tuning gains of hand-crafted reflex networks, injecting correlated exploration noise, combining self-organizing signals like DEP-RL, or reducing action dimensionality through fixed muscle synergies. However, these methods either impose rigid coordination externally or rely on auxiliary controllers only present during training.

The key breakthrough here is changing the control variable. Instead of directly outputting muscle excitation, the policy commands the muscle threshold length $\lambda$ from Feldman's equilibrium-point (EP) hypothesis. While each muscle contracts reflexively based on its own stretch, all muscles are coupled through the skeleton, allowing dynamic skeletal interactions to coordinate the muscles naturally.

sections.heading: How $\lambda$-hold control works: Reflex laws and event-driven intermittent updates
sections.summary: On a 21-DoF, 90-muscle model, the policy decides threshold lengths $\lambda$ intermittently, synchronized with contact events such as heel-strike and toe-off. Between decisions, stretch-reflex recruitment laws continuously generate muscle excitations.
sections.details:
The simulation uses the "H2190" three-dimensional musculoskeletal model, featuring 21 mechanical degrees of freedom and 90 muscle-tendon units, running in SCONE with the Hyfydy physics engine at a step size of $0.01\,$ s.

The core of the framework is the $\lambda$-hold controller. The policy commands a threshold length $\lambda_i \in [0.6, 1.2]$ for each muscle. Muscle excitation $e_i$ is then autonomously evaluated at each simulation step via a stretch-reflex recruitment law:
$e_i = [G_{\mathrm{tonic}}(\ell_i - \lambda_i) + G_{\mathrm{phasic}}[v_i]_+ ]_0^1$
where $\ell_i$ is normalized muscle-fiber length and $v_i$ is normalized lengthening velocity. The tonic reflex gain $G_{\mathrm{tonic}}=50$ and phasic reflex gain $G_{\mathrm{phasic}}=0.1$ are shared and fixed across all 90 muscles. A muscle is strongly recruited in proportion to its stretch only when stretched beyond its threshold $\lambda_i$.

Equally important is the intermittent hold mechanism. The policy is not queried at every simulation step ($0.01\,$ s). Instead, it is invoked on ground reaction force (GRF) events: specifically, whenever vertical GRF on either foot crosses $0.05$ body weight (touchdown and toe-off), along with an interpolated sub-point between them. The newly decided $\lambda$ values are held constant until the next event. Because the policy is queried only about 8 times per stride, computational overhead drops drastically.

The RL algorithm uses Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) combined with generalized State-Dependent Exploration (gSDE). The 432-dimensional observation space consists of biologically plausible sensory inputs—such as muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and vestibular cues—together with the currently held $\lambda$ values.

The reward function is remarkably minimal. It simply scales an exponential reward on forward center-of-mass velocity $v_x$ by a penalty on lateral drift $v_z$:
$r = \exp(v_x) \cdot \exp(-v_z^2 / (2\sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}^2))$
It contains no reference motion to track, no joint limit penalties, and no metabolic energy terms.

captions.F2: Timing of $\lambda$ decisions during high-speed sprinting. The policy generates a new $\lambda$ vector only at touchdown (red lines), toe-off (orange lines), and intermediate sub-points (blue lines), holding values in between. Synchronizing decisions with gait events allows the policy to modulate stride cadence flexibly.

sections.heading: Astonishing learning speed and human-like running from a minimal reward
sections.summary: $\lambda$-hold learned orders of magnitude faster than baselines, reaching a top speed of $4.7\,$ m/s in roughly one hour. The emergent joint kinematics and ground reaction forces align closely with human running data and show strong correlation with electromyographic patterns.
sections.details:
The authors evaluated learning performance against four baselines: Plain SAC controlling excitations directly, Excitation-hold applying intermittent holds to excitations, DEP-RL using self-organizing signals, and a Synergy baseline using low-dimensional latent muscle controls.

- **Orders-of-magnitude faster learning (Section 3.1)**: Across both environment steps and policy decision steps, $\lambda$-hold outperformed all baselines from the very start. Plain SAC and Synergy failed to advance past falling forward within 1–2 steps. DEP-RL stayed upright and moved forward, but plateaued as an unnatural hunched fast walk (around $2.6\,$ m/s). Excitation-hold improved over Plain SAC, but fell far behind $\lambda$-hold. On a single workstation with one GPU, $\lambda$-hold mastered running at roughly $4.0\,$ m/s in just about one hour.

- **Broad joint-space exploration (Section 3.2)**: Examining differential entropy and grid coverage of joint velocities revealed that $\lambda$-hold maintained high entropy from early training onward. Ultimately, it explored roughly 2.5 times more joint-velocity space than DEP-RL and about 7 times more than Plain SAC. Dynamic coupling between muscles translated directly into purposeful joint exploration.

- **Emergence of human-like running from minimal reward (Section 3.3)**: Despite rewarding only forward velocity, a symmetric sprint (peaking at $4.7\,$ m/s) with clean swing-leg retraction emerged naturally. When compared with treadmill running data, sagittal joint angles at the hip, knee, and ankle, as well as vertical GRF profiles, mirrored human waveforms closely.

- **Consistency with biological EMG (Section 3.4)**: Comparing simulated muscle activations with human surface EMG at $5.0\,$ m/s yielded an average correlation coefficient of $r=+0.42$ across 11 muscles. Agreement was exceptionally high in primary propulsive muscles, including the soleus ($r=0.80$) and gastrocnemius (medial $0.87$, lateral $0.83$). This level of fidelity is extraordinary for a controller trained from scratch without trajectory tracking.

captions.F3: Comparison of sprinting learning curves. Plotted against both environment steps (a) and policy decision steps (b), $\lambda$-hold (blue) achieves returns over an order of magnitude higher on a log scale than all baselines.
captions.F4: Comparison of joint-velocity space exploration: (a) differential entropy of visited joint velocity distributions, and (b) number of visited grid cells (coverage). $\lambda$-hold (blue) covers the most diverse and expansive joint-motion space from start to finish.
captions.F5: Comparison between emergent sprinting motions (blue) and human experimental data (dashed). Across speeds of $2.5$, $3.5$, and $4.5\,$ m/s, sagittal joint angles for the hip, knee, and ankle, alongside vertical ground reaction forces (GRF), align remarkably well with human patterns.
captions.F6: Comparison of simulated muscle activations (blue) against recorded human surface EMG (dashed). Triceps surae muscles, such as the soleus and gastrocnemius, show strong correlations exceeding $r > 0.8$.

sections.heading: Why physiological principles structure exploration, and where this goes next
sections.summary: The success of $\lambda$-hold stems from dynamic coupling through the skeleton, which yields state-dependent, adaptive synergy. The paper demonstrates a hierarchical synthesis of the equilibrium-point hypothesis, intermittent control, and optimal feedback control, while diagnosing the root cause of the model's speed limit.
sections.details:
Why is $\lambda$-hold so effective? In muscle space, independent exploration cancels out due to many-to-one mappings. However, synergistic muscles share anatomical actions, causing their lengths and velocities to fluctuate together during movement. Through reflex loops, exploration in $\lambda$ space is converted into mechanically coupled synergistic recruitment. Unlike traditional muscle synergy methods that freeze group relationships into fixed matrices, dynamic interactions through the skeleton produce "living synergies" that naturally adapt to posture and gait phase.

The findings also help bridge classic theoretical divides. Critics of the equilibrium-point (EP) hypothesis have argued that fast, complex tasks would require prohibitively convoluted virtual trajectories, necessitating explicit internal force models, or raised the homunculus problem of where threshold trajectories originate. Here, high-speed sprinting was achieved with only about 8 decisions per stride and a shared reflex law across all muscles, proving that complex virtual trajectories are unnecessary. The system can be understood hierarchically: a learned high-level policy acts as an optimal feedback controller to set threshold targets $\lambda$, while the low-level EP reflex mechanism interacts with skeletal dynamics to generate real forces.

Finally, the model's top speed plateau of $4.7\,$ m/s was not a failure of the controller, but a limitation of the musculoskeletal model itself. During swing-phase hip flexion, the iliopsoas shortens rapidly; due to the intrinsic force-velocity relationship, active muscle tension drops to only $1/4$ to $1/3$ of isometric strength. In addition, the model lacks arms to counterbalance angular momentum.

sections.heading: Appendix: Preventing cyclic catastrophic forgetting and reaching $6.5\,$ m/s
sections.summary: Periodic performance crashes caused by interference between accelerating and high-speed cruising were eliminated using Reference State Initialization (RSI). Furthermore, a curriculum on maximum muscle shortening velocity raised the top sprint speed to $6.5\,$ m/s.
sections.details:
In the main text's learning curves (Figure 3), returns exhibited periodic drops and recoveries late in training. This reflects catastrophic forgetting inherent to multi-task reinforcement learning, where a single policy must balance stationary acceleration against high-speed steady cruising.

- **Stabilization via Reference State Initialization (RSI)**: The authors built an autonomous state archive from high-scoring historical episodes, resetting episodes to high-speed cruising states with a fixed probability. This prevented the policy from forgetting high-speed running skills, yielding smooth, monotonic convergence without oscillations.

- **Curriculum on shortening velocity limit breaks the speed ceiling**: Even after stabilization, top speed stalled around $4.7\,$ m/s because psoas and iliacus shortening velocities spiked during swing, reducing force output via the force-velocity relationship. By applying a curriculum that progressively relaxed the maximum shortening velocity parameter across all muscles (from the standard 10 optimal fiber lengths per second up to 20), sprint speed reached $6.5\,$ m/s. This confirmed that the velocity ceiling stemmed from the physiological model parameters rather than the control framework.

captions.F7: Effects of Reference State Initialization (RSI) and the maximum shortening velocity curriculum. Introducing RSI (green line) eliminates late-stage return oscillations, while the velocity relaxation curriculum (purple line) unlocks even higher returns.

takeaways: In actuator-redundant biological or robotic systems, learning parameters that govern compliance and reflex thresholds (like equilibrium points) yields far more efficient exploration than directly outputting low-level actuation.
Instead of hardcoding whole-body muscle synergies into fixed matrices, flexible synergies emerge naturally from shared reflex laws coupled through skeletal dynamics.
Rather than maximizing control frequency, updating commands intermittently (Hold) based on dynamic contact events is critical for learning stability and computational efficiency.
limitations: Decision timing relies heavily on periodic ground reaction force events (touchdown and toe-off), leaving open whether the scheme transfers directly to non-periodic manipulation or upper-body tasks.
Because the model lacks arms and lower-limb flexors face intrinsic force-velocity limits, it does not yet reach the top speeds of elite human sprinters (over $10\,$ m/s).
While predicted muscle activations match human EMG well during stance propulsion, discrepancies in activation timing remain in some muscles, such as the tibialis anterior during swing phase.
